newsitem.title: UK: Dollar touch softer, digests Jochimsen comments.
newsitem.headline: Dollar touch softer, digests Jochimsen comments.

text.p: The dollar was a shade weaker against the mark and yen in early Europe, depressed after Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said he wouldn't rule out another cut in rates, said analysts.

"It is the first comment we have had from a Bundesbank official for some time suggesting there is still scope for rate cuts and holding out the prospect of further Bundesbank easing," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
But, said Stamenkovic, Jochimsen's comment was tempered by the fact that while saying he did not rule out another cut in rates, he said he did not see one.
At 0835 GMT dollar/mark stood at 1.7240/45 against 1.7252/62 in late Europe on Wednesday. Against the yen, the dollar was steady at 113.98/08 yen against 113.98/08 yen.
Jochimsen, speaking in Frankfurt earlier, said he would not rule out another reduction in Bundesbank interest rates in the present economic cycle but added that he did not see one.
Analysts said overall, however, his comments had failed to give clear direction to the dollar as it now seemed undecided about which way it wanted to trade.
"He didn't really, give the market too much of a clue," said Stamenkovic.
Analysts said a clear commitment to a German rate cut could boost the dollar, but the market on Thursday got mixed signals from Jochimsen.
"I think the Bundesbank is quite content for now to leave policy on hold," said Stamenkovic.

The market also got mixed signals from the Bundesbank's Jochimsen on European monetary union. Jochimsen warned the prospects for EMU were being threatened by the lack of political integration and by a fundamental dissent between Germany and France. Comments like this, said traders, would normally be mark supportive.

But some were also confused as Jochimsen said a postponement to EMU would not necessarily lead to mark appreciation. He also said he was seeing some signs that investors were transferring funds out of the mark ahead of EMU, but that he saw no indications of major shifts.

"Taken as a whole, however, Jochimsen's comments were not necessarily that negative for the mark. In particular, he claimed that the economic and political conditions were not right for EMU and that there was a very real danger of a postponement," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Analysts, moreover, said they expected the dollar only to get clear direction once the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting is over on July 1-2.

"The only thing that will give clear direction to the dollar will be interest-rate expectations once the FOMC meeting is out of the way," said Claudio Demolli, foreign exchange analyst at Merrill Lynch.

Elsewhere, the Bundesbank started its regular fortnightly policy-making meeting on Thursday with economists convinced it would keep rates unchanged despite last week's disappointing M3 money supply data.
In other currencies, the lira rose to five-month highs of 975.70 against the mark. Currency markets are eyeing moves in Italy amid speculation of a rate cut in the near term.
